opus-5.5.text:
I think of it as a ladder of verifiability. Mathematics sits at the top because, especially when you formalize it in something like Lean, you get a perfect verifier. A proof either checks or it doesn't. There's no ambiguity, no human grader having a bad day. That makes math an incredibly clean training ground for reasoning: you can generate attempts, get a crisp signal back, and improve. It's almost like the game of Go, except the space is infinitely richer and actually connected to everything else we care about.

Programming is one step down that ladder. Code can be run, tested, type-checked, so you still get strong feedback, but it's noisier. Tests can be incomplete, specs can be underspecified, and "it runs" isn't the same as "it's correct." What's beautiful is that formal math and programming are converging. A Lean proof *is* a program, and verified software is basically mathematics about code. So progress in one pulls the other forward.

Then there's the real world, where testing is slow, expensive, and messy. You run an experiment in a lab, you deploy something, and the feedback takes weeks and is full of confounders. My view is that you don't get to robust real-world reasoning by starting there. You build the core reasoning capability where verification is cheap and exact, which is math, then extend it to code, where verification is mostly mechanical, and then you push outward into science and engineering, carrying that discipline of "show me the proof, show me the check" with you.

So to me AGI isn't just a model that sounds smart. It's a system that can generate ideas *and* verify them, and math is where you learn to do both honestly. If an AI can produce new, formally verified mathematics, that's a very strong signal it has real reasoning rather than pattern-matched fluency. And that reasoning engine is what eventually lets you trust it in domains where the stakes are physical and the verifier is reality itself.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I think about it as three layers that constantly feed into each other, and I'll try to explain why each one matters.

Mathematics, to me, is the purest test of reasoning. There's no ambiguity in whether a proof is correct. You can't bluff your way through it, you can't rely on surface-level pattern matching, and you can't appeal to the fact that something "sounds right." Either the logical chain holds or it doesn't. So when I think about whether a system is genuinely intelligent, as opposed to just fluent, mathematics is where I look first. It strips away everything except the reasoning itself.

Programming is where that reasoning meets reality for the first time. Code has to run. It has to handle edge cases, interact with systems that already exist, and produce something that actually works. Programming is interesting because it sits between the abstract and the concrete. It's formal enough that you can verify it, but messy enough that it reflects the real world. A lot of what we call "coding ability" in AI is really the ability to take a mathematical idea, a structure, an algorithm, an invariant, and translate it into something executable that doesn't break.

And then real-world testing is the layer that keeps everyone honest. You can have a beautiful theoretical framework and elegant code, and still fail when you deploy it, because the world has constraints you didn't anticipate. Data is noisy. Users behave unexpectedly. Systems interact in ways nobody modeled. That feedback loop, where reality tells you what you got wrong, is irreplaceable. Without it, you're optimizing for your own assumptions rather than for truth.

The reason I see these as connected in an AGI worldview is that intelligence isn't just one of them. A system that can only do math is a very good theorem prover. A system that can only write code is a very good tool. A system that only learns from real-world feedback without a formal backbone can be fooled or drift in strange directions. What makes something feel like general intelligence is the ability to move fluidly across all three, to reason rigorously, implement precisely, and then update honestly when the world pushes back.

I also think there's a deeper point here about verification. One of the biggest challenges with these models is knowing when to trust them. Math gives us proofs. Programming gives us tests. Real-world deployment gives us outcomes. Each is a form of ground truth. If we're building toward systems that are more capable than us in certain domains, we need those verification mechanisms built in from the start, not bolted on afterward. That's why I personally spend so much of my energy on the mathematical side. If we can get machines to reason correctly in the most unforgiving domain we have, I think that gives us a foundation to build everything else on.

astra-6.text:
I think of them as three parts of a feedback loop. Mathematics gives you a way to state assumptions precisely and reason about what follows from them. Programming turns those ideas into something executable. And real-world testing tells you whether the assumptions captured what actually matters.

You can have a beautiful mathematical result that holds under assumptions that don’t survive contact with reality. You can also have a program that performs well without really understanding why it works or where it will fail. So I’d want those three activities to keep informing one another: formulate an idea, implement it, test it, and use the failures to revise the idea.

For AGI, that loop seems especially important. We want systems that can reason abstractly, turn reasoning into actions, and learn when the consequences don’t match their predictions. Mathematics helps make the reasoning rigorous; programming makes it operational; testing keeps it grounded.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of them as three complementary ways of asking whether an idea actually works. Mathematics helps us make our assumptions precise and understand what follows from them. Programming forces us to turn those ideas into something executable. And real-world testing tells us whether the assumptions captured what mattered in the first place.

For AGI, that feedback loop seems essential. You can have a beautiful mathematical framework, but implementing it exposes gaps. You can have a program that performs well on a benchmark, but putting it in a new environment exposes a different set of gaps. Those failures can then lead you back to better mathematical questions.

So I wouldn’t treat any one of the three as sufficient. The goal is to move between abstraction, construction, and observation—to build systems that can reason about a problem, act on that reasoning, and revise their understanding when reality pushes back.
